reviewCards.front: What failure mode does claiming sole credit for a plan like the Pennsylvania Hospital's matching grant risk, and what should trigger you to share credit instead?
reviewCards.back: The Pennsylvania Hospital's matching grant petition worked partly because it wasn't pitched as one man's idea. Claiming sole credit invites envy and resistance from people who resent being led, so the trigger for sharing credit is any moment a proposal needs strangers' trust and money to succeed.

reviewCards.front: What triggered volunteers, not a city office, to organize fire protection the way the Association organized its defense funding through a cannon lottery?
reviewCards.back: The boundary was simple: no official department existed yet, so members had to supply their own leather-bucket gear and inspect it together. The same gap-filling trigger pushed the Association to fund its battery through a cannon lottery once the Assembly's principles blocked direct weapons money.

reviewCards.front: Tracing how pooled annual dues built a shared book collection, what common error do readers make about where that collection actually came from?
reviewCards.back: The trigger was a plain gap: no single reader could afford a wide set of books alone, so pooled annual dues funded the purchase together. The common error is assuming one man donated his personal collection, when trustees and subscribers, the same funding shape later reused for the Academy of Philadelphia, built it instead.

reviewCards.front: What boundary does the Union Fire Company's about-thirty-member start-up put on the claim that one small pilot always guarantees wider adoption?
reviewCards.back: Leather buckets carried by about thirty members proved the mutual-aid idea worked at small scale, but wider adoption still needed separate proof. One paved and lit stretch of street had to earn its own citywide follow-through the same way, since a small working pilot only shows local success, not automatic spread.

reviewCards.front: What sign shows that treating these civic projects as just a list of good deeds misses the real hard edge of what made them work?
reviewCards.back: Restraining personal pride, not charisma or a résumé of good works, is the sign to look for. The same discipline that once tracked private virtues let backers behind projects like the Library Company share credit and lower resistance, since a proposal claimed by one name draws envy that a shared one avoids.

reviewCards.front: Between the Pennsylvania Hospital's matching grant and a straight lottery for artillery money, what decides which funding route to reach for when a governing body won't approve direct funding?
reviewCards.back: The contrast is what the funding is for and why the body refuses: a matching grant works when lawmakers merely doubt an outright gift, since matching private subscription money makes the gift look proven, while a cannon lottery works when the block is a principled refusal to fund weapons at all, so it raises the money entirely outside the assembly's vote.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: When a proposal is ready to leave your small planning circle, draft it two ways: one naming you as sole originator, one reading as if it comes from a small group. The same shift let trustees carry the Academy of Philadelphia's subscription drive forward using a template already proven elsewhere. Show both versions to one person who wasn't in the planning meeting and ask which they'd back, then write down the specific condition under which you'd send the shared-credit version again, so the repeat condition is something someone outside the room can check, not just something you remember.

ifThenPlans.context: Before you send a proposal that currently carries your name only
ifThenPlans.plan: If the draft credits you alone, then write a second version crediting 'a few of us' the way Union Fire Company's roughly thirty members shared ownership of their leather buckets and duty roster, and post the condition for reusing either version on a note that someone who wasn't in the planning meeting can read.

ifThenPlans.context: Before you hand a proven pitch template to a new project without checking who owns it
ifThenPlans.plan: If no one has agreed to own the follow-through, then name one person as owner in writing, the way trustees owned the Academy of Philadelphia's subscription drive, or refuse to launch the template. Log the named-owner choice against the no-owner choice on a shared note so someone who missed the planning meeting can see the reuse condition.

ifThenPlans.context: Before you apply a fixed personal rule about always naming yourself or always staying anonymous
ifThenPlans.plan: If you catch yourself defaulting to that fixed rule, then scope it to this one proposal only. Compare a solo-credit line against a shared-credit line for this single pitch, and write the boundary you set on a note visible to someone who wasn't in the planning meeting.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take the pitch from your two-minute audit and actually send it twice today: once naming yourself, once framed as coming from a few people, the same choice that let trustees reuse the Academy of Philadelphia's fundraising template instead of building one from scratch. Then write down which version got a yes fastest.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, scan your calendar for any pitch, ask, or announcement you're about to repeat, and check whether it's still credited to you alone or to the group backing it. Adjust the framing before you send it again, and keep a running note of which framing keeps getting more yeses.

memorableLines.text: The Union Fire Company ran on leather buckets, not tax dollars.
Library Company subscribers paid annual dues to buy books together.
Backers behind the Academy of Philadelphia recruited trustees.

chapters.title: Part Four
chapters.hook: Franklin walked out of Lord Granville's chamber having just learned a hard rule: a king's instruction binds a colonial governor as law, full stop.
chapters.counterintuition: Colonists believed their assemblies stood as Legislator of the Colonies, equal to Parliament under charter; the crown's law ran straight through the governor instead, no vote required.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one request that's stalled because you keep asking the person who is friendly, not the one who holds actual authority over it. Franklin ran into this against Thomas Penn's estate: pressing his case in person earned sympathy, but only a written complaint routed to the body with jurisdiction (the process behind his Heads of Complaint) produced a documented review, even though the underlying dispute was never resolved. Today, name who actually holds authority over your stalled request, and send that person one written ask stating what you need and by when. Track whether you get a dated response, not whether the answer is yes.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Franklin's only power in London was patience and reputation. No title moved Granville, Paris, or Loudoun. The tax fight stayed open when his memoir broke off.

breakdown.fastRead:
Franklin sailed to England as agent for the Pennsylvania Assembly. This was no fun trip. In London, Lord Granville gave him a hard, plain rule: a king's word to a governor stands as law. Franklin had thought the Assembly held the same say as Parliament, under its own charter. Granville's words knocked that idea down flat.

The fight was over money. Thomas Penn's family kept their own proprietary estates free of tax, while every other landholder paid to help fund the war. Franklin wrote out the Assembly's complaint and filed it with the men in London who handled such cases. Ferdinand John Paris, the proprietors' solicitor, fought back hard. He treated each letter like an enemy's move, not a fair ask.

The case stayed open for years. Franklin's own memoir stops mid-fight. He died in 1790 before he could finish the tale.
breakdown.deepRead:
Before Franklin could even sail, he had to wait on Lord Loudoun. Lord Loudoun commanded troops in New York. Every day he said the same thing: the dispatches would be ready tomorrow. The packet boat sat in port for weeks, going nowhere. Franklin came to see the real cause. Loudoun was warm and quick in talk, but he could not close a choice and be done with it.

London brought a bigger test. Lord Granville, President of the Privy Council, met with Franklin early on. Granville said plainly that a governor must obey the king's word as law, no charter could change that. Franklin had thought the Assembly stood as Legislator of the Colonies, with the same say as Parliament. Granville's flat claim knocked that belief down at once.

The dispute itself was simple to state. Thomas Penn and the rest of his family kept their proprietary estates free of tax, even as the Assembly taxed every other landholder to help pay for the war with France. Franklin wrote out the Assembly's complaint and carried it to the men in London who reviewed such cases.

Ferdinand John Paris, the proprietors' solicitor, read every complaint as a legal threat, then answered with sharp words built to slow the case down. The clash between the two men turned personal, not just formal, and it stretched the fight for years.

None of Franklin's old wins back home bought him any pull here. Not over a commander's calendar. Not over a royal official's claim. Not over a hostile solicitor's pen. Only his good name and his will to keep showing up moved things at all, and even that took years of referrals and written opinions with no ruling in sight. The case was still open, headed toward the crown's own review, when Franklin's memoir stops mid-fight. He died in 1790 before he could write the end.
breakdown.fullRead:
Franklin did not sail to England for himself. The Pennsylvania Assembly sent him as its agent, with one plain job: press its case against the colony's own landowning family until someone with real power settled it. Nothing he had built at home carried any weight here. He held no office that made anyone answer to him. Every person he met in London held power he did not, and every step forward came from patience and a good name, never from rank.

The trip almost never started. Lord Loudoun commanded troops in New York and kept telling Franklin the dispatches would be ready tomorrow. Tomorrow came, then the next one, week after week. The commander held the only paper that could send the boat out, and until he signed it, nobody could sail. Lord Loudoun let the packet boat sit idle for weeks. Franklin watched the pattern and named it plainly: a man warm and quick in talk, who could open any conversation but close none of them. Wind and tide had nothing to do with it.

London gave him no easier start. Lord Granville, President of the Privy Council, met Franklin early and set him straight: a king's word to a governor carries the weight of law, whatever a colony's charter claims. In London's own view, a colony's charter meant nothing next to a royal order. Franklin had crossed the ocean sure the Assembly held its own say, the way Parliament held its own say at home. Lord Granville said no colony's assembly stood as Legislator of the Colonies. One flat sentence knocked that belief down.

The fight he carried into that world was plain to state and hard to end. Thomas Penn kept his proprietary estates free of tax through the whole war, even while every other landholder in the colony paid in full. The Penns wanted their own ground left alone while asking everyone else to pay for the guns. Franklin wrote out the Assembly's complaint and carried it to the men in London who reviewed such cases. It was a formal paper aimed at a formal body, not a quiet word passed between neighbors.

Waiting on the other end of every letter sat Ferdinand John Paris, the proprietors' solicitor. He met each complaint as an attack to beat back, not a claim to weigh, and he answered with sharp words built to slow things down, not to settle them. Defending the family's money was his whole job, and treating every complaint as a threat served it well. The friction between the two men ran personal, not just formal, and that alone stretched the fight well past what the facts alone would have required.

None of it closed on any single day. No single person in this fight could force the others to agree, so the case crawled from one committee to the next. The case moved through years of referrals and written opinions, never one clean meeting. Franklin's work had shifted from building things at home to arguing, abroad, for men who owed Pennsylvania nothing at all. The case was still open, headed toward the crown's own review, when Franklin's memoir stops in the middle of the fight. He died in 1790 before he could write the end.

examples.title: Whose Number She's Carrying
examples.scenario: Zoe carries one signed sheet into a diner booth on her lunch break, sent by the co-op board to lock in next year's dues before the landlord's meeting. Russell guesses she's floating her own number and offers a private trade instead: a lower rate in exchange for reserved parking. Gaelle backs him, sure the real decision hasn't started yet. Zoe sets the board's authorization on the table and says the figure isn't hers to bargain; she was sent to carry it, not invent it. She thinks of Lord Granville telling Franklin, in words to this effect, that a governor's word alone settled the matter, as if he spoke for the whole Legislator of the Colonies by himself. Russell and Gaelle drop the side deal only once the signed sheet is actually on the table.
examples.whatToDo: When someone offers a private side term to a person carrying a group's mandate, that person should decline to answer for themselves and send the offer back to whoever authorized them, in writing, before any number changes.
examples.whyItMatters: Franklin's crossing carried the Pennsylvania Assembly's grievance, not an errand of his own; a mandate that bends the moment someone offers a private trade was never a real mandate, and testing it before commitment protects the person holding it as much as the group behind it.

examples.title: Tracking Every Broken Tomorrow
examples.scenario: Russell is running his first vendor sign-off, tracking each promised approval for the annual dues mailing on a sticky note above his monitor. The print manager tells him Tuesday that the artwork will clear tomorrow. Wednesday comes, then more days of the same word. Russell assumes a supply problem is holding the ink order, until he calls the supplier directly and hears nothing is backordered at all: the manager alone just hasn't signed off. The surprise lands hard: the holdup was never materials, only a man who can't close a decision and say either yes or no. Russell thinks of Lord Loudoun holding Franklin in New York with the same tomorrow, week after week, while the packet boat sat waiting. The mailing goes out late, and Russell stops treating a cheerful tomorrow as an answer.
examples.whatToDo: When a promised go-ahead keeps sliding by a day, stop asking for tomorrow and ask instead for a fixed date in writing, or route the approval through someone else who can actually close it.
examples.whyItMatters: The delay wasn't the packet boat, and it wasn't the ink order, both times the holdup was one person's inability to finalize anything, and mistaking that for a logistics problem only stretches the wait.

examples.title: A Proposal That Skips the Owner's Plot
examples.scenario: Gaelle texts her friend a first draft of the shared garden-plot proposal: get the city's sign-off, then split upkeep evenly among growers. Her friend texts back fast: the fight was never going to be with the city. It's going to be with the building's owner, who keeps a private bed inside the co-op's own fenced yard and has never paid toward it. Gaelle's draft doesn't mention the owner's plot at all, and when she posts it that afternoon, the owner objects loudly to being taxed on his own land. Her friend texts that it sounds like the Penn fight all over again, Thomas Penn keeping his own proprietary estates off the tax rolls while ordinary tenants paid theirs. Gaelle rewrites the proposal that night, naming the owner's plot directly instead of assuming everyone already agrees who owes what.
examples.whatToDo: Before circulating a shared-cost proposal, name every party expected to pay, including whoever already holds a private exemption inside the shared space, so the objection surfaces before the vote instead of after it.
examples.whyItMatters: The dispute the Assembly carried to London was never about outside taxation, it was whether the Penns' own land inside the colony would be taxed like everyone else's, and skipping that question only moves the argument later instead of avoiding it.

examples.title: The Doodle in the Corner of the Clipboard
examples.scenario: Every closing shift, Skylar leaves the day's counts for Kira to review the next morning. For weeks she assumes the red-inked corrections piling up mean Kira is just slow and overloaded, until Anna, who closes the same shift some evenings, says otherwise: Kira answers every note like a complaint to be knocked down, never information to use. The two of them start leaving a small doodle in the corner of the shared clipboard before handoff, something for the next closer to find. What was a dreaded handoff becomes the one real conversation Skylar has all day, waiting to see what Anna left. Skylar says it reminds her of Ferdinand John Paris, proprietors' solicitor, meeting every letter from the Assembly as an attack to answer, never a problem to fix. Kira does the same to a stock count.
examples.whatToDo: Before handing a routine report to someone who reads every note as a challenge, cc a second colleague who will read it as information instead, so the handoff carries real feedback and not just another objection to answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The proprietors' solicitor wasn't slow, he was choosing to fight every complaint on principle; naming hostility instead of laziness is what let Skylar and Anna build a workaround instead of waiting for it to pass.

examples.title: One Nod Is Not a Vote
examples.scenario: Kira pins a notice to the club corkboard the same afternoon the officers' meeting ends: dues rules changed, effective immediately. She'd gotten one officer's nod and figured that settled it. By evening, three members have pulled the notice down and posted their own, asking who actually approved it, since the treasurer never signed off and the full board hasn't voted. Kira has to print a second notice walking the change back to proposed, pinned right over her first one. She thinks of Lord Granville announcing, as the record has it, that a governor's instructions bound the colonies no matter what an assembly believed, as though he alone were the Legislator of the Colonies. The same overreach Kira had just made: one voice standing in for a decision nobody else had reached.
examples.whatToDo: When posting a group decision as final, confirm the specific body with sign-off, not just one willing voice, has actually voted, and note that on the posting itself.
examples.whyItMatters: The tax dispute took years of referrals and opinions, not one meeting where someone stated a position; treating an early answer as the final one is exactly what forced Kira's public correction.

examples.title: Filing It Herself, Not on Her Name
examples.scenario: Anna has organized three fundraiser runs for the club and figures the parks office will fast-track her weekend request the same way the club always does. Zoe, mapping the course with her Saturday morning, stops circling water-stop locations and says it plainly: none of those past runs put Anna's name on anything the parks office recognizes, and the permit desk will ask her for the same paperwork it asks a stranger for. Anna pushes back, listing every event she's pulled off, but Zoe stays with it instead of dropping it, walking through exactly which office holds sign-off and what it needs by Friday. It landed the way Franklin's own record of founded institutions never bought him standing with the proprietors over the Heads of Complaint sitting before the Board: reputation moved people, never the paperwork on proprietary estates. Anna files the request that afternoon instead of waiting on her name to do the work.
examples.whatToDo: When past success tempts a shortcut around the standard process, name the specific office or person who holds sign-off and route the request through them in writing, the same way anyone else would, before the deadline.
examples.whyItMatters: None of Franklin's founded institutions gave him power over the military commander, the crown official, or the proprietors; reputation opened doors, but only the paperwork moved the decision, and that gap is what Zoe made Anna face before the weekend ran out.

questions.prompt: A regional office insists local custom overrides a headquarters directive, and its outside counsel treats every inquiry from headquarters as an opposing legal filing to counter, the same posture Ferdinand John Paris held as the proprietors' solicitor toward the assembly's complaints. What quick check tests whether the directive itself controls the outcome?
choices: Ask counsel directly whether the directive binds the office, since a hostile lawyer's own answer settles what authority headquarters can actually claim.
Find a documented case where the directive was enforced against another office, then check whether that office complied without dispute.
Escalate straight to the parent board, since counsel's combative replies already prove the directive cannot settle the dispute alone.
questions.explanation: The rule that royal instructions bind a governor as law is the force actually deciding this kind of dispute, not a lawyer's combative tone. Ferdinand John Paris, the proprietors' solicitor, only slowed the case with adversarial replies; testing the directive's own enforcement record isolates which force drives the outcome, instead of taking either side's posture at face value.

questions.prompt: A colleague reports a vendor dispute is basically settled after a private phone call, but for weeks the vendor's manager keeps promising a signed agreement by tomorrow, the same pattern Lord Loudoun used in New York before the packet boat could ever leave port. What shows the dispute isn't actually settled, and what should the team do next?
choices: Read the recurring 'tomorrow' promise as ordinary negotiation delay, since private paperwork often takes several days before a deal closes.
Trust the private phone call as the settlement itself, since a verbal agreement between managers typically counts as binding once spoken.
Treat the recurring broken promise as proof nothing is settled, and route the dispute to the formal review body, not private assurances.
questions.explanation: Lord Loudoun's repeated ready-tomorrow promise in New York never produced the packet boat's departure, showing that a spoken promise is not a finalized action. The assembly's actual complaints were resolved only by formal presentation to the bodies overseeing colonial affairs in London, not by a private assurance between two parties.

questions.prompt: An archivist finds a diplomatic memoir that stops right after an official like Lord Granville states his position, with no verdict on record. Before treating the case as closed, what should the archivist do first?
choices: Check outside records for what happened next, since an abrupt stop can reflect the writer's limits, not a settled outcome.
Conclude the dispute favored the official, since the memoir halts right after he states his firm position on the matter.
Reach out personally to the official's family for their account of the ending, since personal memory usually fills in a missing record.
questions.explanation: Franklin's memoir breaks off mid-negotiation not because the dispute was won or lost, but because he died in 1790 before finishing it, the same way Lord Granville's flat statement left Franklin's Legislator of the Colonies assumption unsettled without a recorded outcome. External records, not assumption, are the only way to learn what came next.

questions.prompt: A staffer is sent overseas by an organization to press a formal grievance about a partner's proprietary estates being kept exempt from a shared cost, the way Thomas Penn's estates were exempted from wartime taxes the assembly needed. Which boundary distinguishes this trip from a personal visit made on the staffer's own reputation?
choices: Any travel abroad counts as official business whenever the traveler already has a public reputation to draw on for access.
The trip stays personal until the organization formally reviews and approves whatever outcome the staffer happens to reach while still abroad.
The trip counts as official because the organization formally appointed the staffer to carry its grievance, not personal fame.
questions.explanation: Franklin crossed the Atlantic as an appointed agent of the Pennsylvania Assembly, sent specifically to press the grievance over Thomas Penn's proprietary estates staying exempt from the tax needed for defense. The formal appointment, not his personal fame, is what made the mission official.

questions.prompt: A shipment sits at dock for weeks while the yard manager keeps saying it will clear customs tomorrow, and teammates blame the delay on customs backlog, the sort of excuse Ferdinand John Paris used when he treated the proprietors' complaints as legal threats instead of backlog. What is the correct next step once the pattern of daily broken promises becomes clear?
choices: Stop waiting on the manager's promise and escalate directly to someone who can authorize the shipment, since the delay is indecision.
Keep checking in with the manager every morning for an updated timeline, since daily follow-up is the standard way shipments eventually clear.
File a formal customs complaint about backlog processing, since a documented complaint usually speeds up an overloaded clearance queue.
questions.explanation: The dock delay follows the same pattern as Franklin's own experience: a promise renewed every day without ever producing the paperwork signals someone unwilling to finalize a decision, not backlog or weather. Ferdinand John Paris showed the same underlying stall tactic as the proprietors' solicitor, answering every complaint as a threat to slow things down rather than settle them. Naming the real cause and going around the promiser moves a stalled matter forward; repeating the daily check-in does not.

questions.prompt: While waiting for a partner corporation's response, a wait dragging on with the same daily ready-tomorrow promises Lord Loudoun gave before the packet boat could leave New York, a task force must classify a cost dispute. The partner's own facilities have stayed exempt from a shared maintenance fee that every other site pays. Is this a dispute with a federal regulator or with the partner itself?
choices: Hold off classifying the dispute until the partner's response finally arrives, since acting before all facts are in risks a wrong call.
Classify it as a dispute with the partner itself, since the partner's own exempt facilities are the actual conflict, not a regulator's rule.
Classify it as a dispute with the federal regulator, since any fee exemption ultimately traces back to regulatory policy set above the partner.
questions.explanation: The core fight was never with Parliament or the crown directly; the proprietor family kept its own landholdings inside the colony exempt from the tax every other landholder paid, an intra-colonial dispute. Lord Loudoun's stalling in New York before the packet boat could sail is a separate delay and says nothing about who the dispute is actually with.

questions.prompt: After a counterpart's lawyer answers every proposal with sharp rebuttals built to slow the deal down, a colleague suggests it's just standard bureaucratic caution that will ease up soon, the same reassurance one might reach for after hearing an official like Lord Granville flatly reject an assumption about legislative standing. Given only the sharp, personally pointed rebuttals as evidence, which read should the team choose?
choices: Trust that the rebuttals are ordinary caution and will soften once the lawyer better understands the proposal's intent and value.
Read the rebuttals as personally antagonistic opposition, not routine caution, since sharp pointed replies to every letter match active resistance.
Assume the rebuttals reflect a backlog of unrelated cases at the lawyer's firm, since heavy caseloads often produce delayed and terse replies.
questions.explanation: A hostile counterpart answering every complaint with sharp, personally pointed rebuttals is opposition, not routine caution, the same blunt directness Lord Granville used when he told Franklin flatly that a governor must obey the king's word as law, unsettling his Legislator of the Colonies assumption. Tone and pattern, not comfort, are the evidence to weigh.

questions.prompt: A startup founder expects a zoning dispute over exempt land, much like Thomas Penn's proprietary estates staying exempt from the tax every other landholder paid, to close after one persuasive meeting with the planning board. What should the founder actually expect, based on how the assembly's own tax dispute played out?
choices: Expect years of committee referrals and written opinions before any ruling, since the exempt proprietary estates dispute followed that slow path.
Expect a ruling within a few weeks once the board reviews the founder's written proposal, since planning boards usually move faster than legislatures.
Expect the dispute to resolve immediately in the meeting itself, since a clear, well-argued case typically persuades a board on the spot.
questions.explanation: The assembly's complaint over Thomas Penn's proprietary estates never closed in one sitting; it moved through years of committee referrals and written opinions with no ruling in sight, and the case was still open when the memoir breaks off. A single persuasive meeting was never how this kind of dispute resolved.

questions.prompt: A well-known engineer moves to a new division and expects her reputation to carry weight with the division's outside counsel, who answers every one of her formal proposals as an opposing filing to counter, much as Ferdinand John Paris did toward the assembly as the proprietors' solicitor. What should trigger her to stop relying on her prior standing and start relying on patience and repeated engagement instead?
choices: Track how many proposals counsel rejects each month, since a rising rejection count alone proves prior standing has stopped working.
Wait until counsel personally acknowledges her reputation, since formal recognition from the opposing side signals when standing has taken hold.
Notice that counsel answers her proposals as filings to counter, not claims to weigh, and shift toward steady persuasion.
questions.explanation: None of Franklin's civic wins back home carried weight with Ferdinand John Paris, the proprietors' solicitor, who answered every complaint as a legal threat regardless of Franklin's reputation, and only patience and repeated engagement moved the case at all. The signal to drop reliance on standing is the pattern of the response, not a count of rejections.

reviewCards.front: What failure mode did Lord Granville's claim about royal instructions expose in Franklin's assumption about colonial charters?
reviewCards.back: Lord Loudoun's stalling in New York, keeping the packet boat from sailing for weeks, was one instance of Franklin's plans depending on someone else's decision he could not compel. In London the same power gap showed clearer: Lord Granville stated flatly that a king's instruction binds a governor as law, exposing the wrong assumption that colonial charters gave assemblies equal legislative standing.

reviewCards.front: What triggers a colonial assembly's grievance to move from a local complaint into a formal London review?
reviewCards.back: Once a dispute can't be settled directly between the two parties, it crosses into formal channels: the assembly's complaints against the proprietors were compiled and carried to the bodies in London reviewing colonial affairs, the same world where Lord Granville had already told Franklin that a governor's instructions carry the weight of law, undercutting any claim the assembly stood as Legislator of the Colonies on equal footing.

reviewCards.front: Why does the tax fight over Thomas Penn's proprietary estates never reach a stated resolution on the page?
reviewCards.back: The trigger is Franklin's own death in 1790, not a decision by either side: the assembly's case against Thomas Penn's proprietary estates was still moving through committee referrals when the memoir simply stops. A common error reads the abrupt ending as a deliberate close or a settlement, when it only reflects an unfinished manuscript.

reviewCards.front: What does the standoff with Ferdinand John Paris teach about the boundary between an official mission and a personal visit?
reviewCards.back: Appointment is the concrete boundary: Franklin crossed the Atlantic as the Pennsylvania Assembly's named agent, not on his own account, which is exactly why he had standing to file a formal complaint at all. Ferdinand John Paris, the proprietors' solicitor, answered that complaint as an opposing legal filing, a response that only makes sense against a formally appointed party, not a private visitor.

reviewCards.front: What diagnostic sign shows that Lord Loudoun's delay in New York came from indecision, not weather or logistics?
reviewCards.back: Watch the pattern, not the excuse: Lord Loudoun, commanding troops in New York, kept promising the packet boat's dispatches would be ready tomorrow for weeks, and the boat never once left port on that promise. The hard edge is that Franklin read this as a fixed trait, not bad weather or a logistics snag.

reviewCards.front: Is the tax dispute Franklin carries to London a fight with Parliament over colonial taxation, or a fight with the proprietors over their own exempt land?
reviewCards.back: The contrast is intra-colonial versus imperial: the dispute is not with Parliament over taxing the colonies from outside, it's with the Penn family over their own proprietary land staying exempt while the assembly taxes every other landholder for defense. Lord Granville's separate claim, that a governor must obey royal instructions as law regardless of colonial charter, undercut the assembly's Legislator of the Colonies standing, but that fight is distinct from the tax dispute itself.

reviewCards.front: Under what condition does a legal opponent's slow reply signal active antagonism instead of ordinary bureaucratic caution?
reviewCards.back: The failure mode is mistaking sharp intent for neutral delay: replies that answer every letter as a legal threat, built specifically to slow resolution, mark personal opposition, not routine backlog. That is the pattern the proprietors' solicitor showed toward the assembly's complaint over Thomas Penn's proprietary estates, treating each filing as an attack to defeat instead of a grievance to weigh.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is a stakeholder interview: before you approve any escalation, sit down with the specific person whose response has to change and ask what would move their decision. A written request to whoever holds actual authority does not guarantee a fast yes (Franklin's own case moved to formal review without ever reaching a settled outcome), but it produces a dated record you can act on next. Close every review by confirming you can name that person.

ifThenPlans.context: When a stalled decision keeps sitting with someone who is easy to reach but slow to decide
ifThenPlans.plan: If that person keeps sliding the timeline, then stop, name exactly who has actual say over the decision, and interview that person directly about what would move their answer; approve no next step until you can name whose response has to change, and if no one will own it, ask for a formal refusal instead of another vague yes.

ifThenPlans.context: When a rule gets invoked to block your entire request instead of just the part it actually covers
ifThenPlans.plan: If a broad rule is used to shut down the whole ask, then interview whoever is invoking it about the exact boundary of what it covers, write the narrowest version of your request that fits inside that boundary, and route only that narrower ask to whoever has standing to approve it, then approve the move once you can name whose response has to change.

ifThenPlans.context: After a written request passes its deadline with no reply
ifThenPlans.plan: If the deadline passes with no answer, then treat the silence as a missed signal, not a resolution: return to the person you interviewed, confirm in writing that the matter is still open, and name who should respond next before you approve any further move.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, run one stakeholder interview: pick your most-stalled ask, find the person who actually has authority over it (not the one easiest to reach), and ask them directly what needs to happen for a decision. Write down their answer and the date. Approve no next step until you can name whose response has to change.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, hold one recurring conversation with whoever currently owns your stalled ask, confirm whether their answer has changed, and update your written note with the date and outcome: even 'still no answer' counts as a result worth recording.

memorableLines.text: Lord Loudoun commanded troops in New York.
Lord Granville said no colony's assembly stood as Legislator of the Colonies.
Ferdinand John Paris, the proprietors' solicitor, fought back hard.
